A Note on This Piece: What follows is a persuasive essay written to advocate one position on a deeply contested moral and political question. It presents the strongest case for unrestricted abortion access and does not attempt to give equal weight to opposing views, many of which are held sincerely and thoughtfully by reasonable people.

The Body Is Not Public Property

There is a principle so basic to human dignity that we rarely bother to articulate it: your body belongs to you. Not to your family, not to your community, not to the state. It is the one piece of the world that is unambiguously and inalienably yours, because it is not merely something you possess—it is what you are. Every argument for restricting abortion, however carefully dressed in the language of compassion or compromise, ultimately requires abandoning this principle. It requires declaring that a pregnant person's body becomes, for some period of time, a resource the government may conscript. Once we accept that, we have not made a small exception. We have surrendered the whole idea.

The Law Already Knows This

Consider how absolute bodily autonomy is everywhere else in law and ethics.

A man dies in a hospital. His kidneys could save two lives, his liver a third, his heart a fourth. He did not sign a donor card. The state does not take his organs. A corpse retains stronger protection against bodily conscription than we would grant a living, breathing pregnant woman under abortion restrictions.

A child needs a bone marrow transplant. Her father is the only compatible donor. The procedure is uncomfortable but not dangerous. No court in any liberal democracy will compel him. In McFall v. Shimp, an American court explicitly refused to force a man to donate marrow to a dying cousin, calling such compulsion a change that would "raise the spectre of the swastika." The judge thought the man's refusal morally repugnant. He ordered nothing.

You cannot be forced to give blood, though the needle takes ten minutes and the risk is essentially zero, and though blood shortages kill people every year. You cannot be forced to undergo surgery for another's benefit. You cannot be forced to submit to a medical procedure at all, even one that would save your own life.

Against this backdrop, pregnancy restrictions are not a modest regulation. They are a singular exception carved out for one class of people, demanding of them a level of bodily sacrifice we demand of no one else in any other circumstance: nine months of profound physiological transformation, permanent alterations to the body, significant medical risk, and a delivery that in the United States kills roughly twenty-two women per hundred thousand live births—many times the mortality risk of abortion at any stage. We do not require a stranger to donate plasma. We would require this.

Even If the Fetus Is a Person

The most common response is that the fetus is a person, and personhood changes everything. Let us grant it—not as a concession of fact but as a demonstration that the argument does not depend on the question.

Judith Jarvis Thomson's famous thought experiment remains unanswered. You wake to find a celebrated violinist plugged into your circulatory system; he will die if unplugged, and he needs nine months. He is unquestionably a person with a full right to life. Are you obligated to remain in that bed? Would the government be justified in strapping you there? Most people, on reflection, say no—and in saying no they concede the crucial point. A right to life is not a right to another person's body. It never has been. The violinist's death, should you unplug, is a tragedy; it is not a murder, because you were never his life support by obligation.

The right to life means the right not to be unjustly killed. It has never meant the right to commandeer another's organs, blood, and physiology for three quarters of a year. To claim otherwise for the fetus alone is to invent a right that exists nowhere else in moral philosophy, and to assign the corresponding duty exclusively to people who can become pregnant.

Why "Any Stage" Is Not an Extreme Position

Here the objection sharpens: perhaps early abortion, but surely not late. Surely a line must exist.

Ask who draws it, and with what knowledge. Viability—the most popular line—is not a moral fact but a technological artifact. It has moved from roughly 28 weeks to 22 in a few decades, and it varies by hospital, by country, by wealth. A fetus is "viable" in Boston and not in rural Bolivia. If the moral status of a pregnancy depends on the neonatal intensive care unit nearest to you, it is not moral status we are measuring. It is infrastructure.

More importantly, consider what gestational limits actually do in the world. Abortions after 21 weeks constitute well under one percent of all abortions. They are not casual. They are the pregnancies where a scan at 22 weeks reveals a fetus with no skull, or lungs that will never inflate, or a condition that guarantees a short life of pain. They are the pregnancies where a woman's heart begins to fail, or her cancer is discovered, or her water breaks at 20 weeks and infection sets in. They are the fourteen-year-old who did not know she was pregnant, and the woman who spent four months and every dollar she had trying to reach a clinic across two state lines.

Into these situations, gestational limits insert a lawyer. Doctors in states with such limits now describe waiting for patients to become sick enough to qualify for an exception—waiting for the sepsis to declare itself, for the bleeding to reach a threshold that will satisfy a hospital's legal counsel. Women have died in that waiting room. This is the actual, documented, empirical consequence of asking the state to draw lines through pregnancy: not fewer tragedies, but tragedies with paperwork.

The people in these rooms—the pregnant person, her doctor, whomever she chooses to consult—possess every relevant fact. Legislators possess none. There is no argument from competence for government involvement, only an argument from authority, and authority over another person's body is precisely what we have no right to claim.

Freedom Is Not Conditional on Approval

Every restriction on abortion is, at bottom, a claim that a pregnant person's judgment about her own body must be ratified by strangers before it becomes valid. Notice that this is not how we treat anyone regarding any other decision of comparable gravity. A person may refuse chemotherapy and die. A person may donate a kidney to a stranger, accepting real surgical risk for no personal benefit. A person may join the military, climb K2, or decline a ventilator. We do not audit these choices for adequate reasons, because the reasons are not ours to audit. Autonomy that only holds when others approve of your decision is not autonomy. It is permission.

And permission systems, once built, do not stay small. They require the state to know who is pregnant, to investigate miscarriages, to subpoena search histories and menstrual apps, to interrogate doctors. Absolute autonomy is not merely the more just position; it is the only position that does not require a surveillance apparatus pointed at the intimate lives of half the population.

Conclusion

There is no version of abortion restriction that does not rest on a single premise: that the government may claim a right to another human being's internal organs. Strip away the gestational tables and the exception clauses and the compromise language, and that premise sits there, unaltered, at the foundation.

We should refuse it. Not because pregnancy is trivial, not because the questions are easy, and not because every choice made in that space is one we would make. We should refuse it because a person who does not own her own body owns nothing at all—and because a free society does not get to decide, on her behalf, what she owes from the inside of her own skin.

Framing

What follows is a steelman of the "no legal restrictions" position, presented from the inside — the reasoning as its proponents would articulate it. It's one position in a contested debate with serious counterarguments; I'm laying it out as requested rather than endorsing it.

The Foundational Premise: Bodily Sovereignty

The core claim is that control over one's own body is not merely one right among many but the precondition for all others. A person who can be compelled to use their organs, blood, and physiology to sustain another entity is, in a meaningful sense, not a free person.

The consistency argument from existing law. In virtually every other context, Anglo-American law refuses to compel bodily use for another's benefit — even to save a life, even when the burden is trivial, even when the person needing help is unambiguously a person. McFall v. Shimp (1978) is the standard citation: a Pennsylvania court refused to order a man to donate bone marrow to his dying cousin, calling compelled donation a change that would "raise the specter of the swastika." Courts do not order blood donations. They do not order kidney donations from parents to children. They do not even harvest organs from corpses without prior consent.

Proponents argue that pregnancy is the sole exception carved out — and that it applies to exactly one class of people. From this vantage, abortion restrictions don't extend equal protection to fetuses; they subtract a protection everyone else enjoys from women and other people who can become pregnant.

Judith Jarvis Thomson's move. The 1971 "violinist" thought experiment is central because of what it concedes: suppose the fetus is a full person with a full right to life. Thomson argues this still doesn't generate a right to use another person's body without consent. A right to life is a right not to be unjustly killed — not a right to whatever is needed to stay alive, including another person's organs. This lets the position sidestep the metaphysics of personhood entirely, which proponents see as its great strength: you don't have to win the argument about when life begins.

Why No Gestational Limits Specifically

This is where the position becomes distinctive, and its defenders offer several lines of reasoning.

Line-drawing is arbitrary and unprincipled. Viability is the most common proposed line, but it shifts with technology (from ~28 weeks to ~22 weeks within living memory) and varies by geography — a fetus "viable" near a well-resourced NICU in Boston is not viable in rural Mali. A right that appears and disappears based on hospital infrastructure, proponents argue, is not tracking any morally real property of the fetus. Heartbeat, brain activity, and quickening fare no better as bright lines; each is a continuous developmental process arbitrarily frozen at a legislative moment.

The autonomy principle doesn't decay. If bodily sovereignty is the ground, it doesn't attenuate at week 20 or 24. The burden of pregnancy in fact increases with time — physically, medically, and in terms of risk. Childbirth carries substantially higher mortality risk than abortion at any gestational stage.

Restrictions target the hardest cases. Empirically, abortions after 21 weeks constitute roughly 1% of the U.S. total. They are overwhelmingly cases of severe or lethal fetal anomalies (many detectable only at the 20-week anatomy scan), catastrophic maternal health emergencies, or people who were delayed by the very barriers that restrictions create — cost, travel, waiting periods, finding a provider. The argument is that late restrictions function almost entirely as traps for people in tragedy, not as a check on some population of casually procrastinating patients. The feared "elective third-trimester abortion" is, on this account, a phantom that legislation invents in order to justify itself.

Exceptions don't work in practice. This is perhaps the most heavily emphasized practical claim. Statutory exceptions for "life of the mother" or "medical emergency" require physicians to guess how close to death a patient must be before intervention becomes legal, under threat of felony prosecution and license loss. Documented cases from Ireland (Savita Halappanavar), Poland, and multiple U.S. states since 2022 involve patients with previable premature rupture of membranes or sepsis being made to wait until deterioration was severe enough to satisfy legal ambiguity. Proponents argue that no drafting can fix this: medicine is probabilistic and time-sensitive, law is categorical and retrospective. The only exception that reliably works is no restriction at all.

The Anti-State-Intervention Dimension

This strand of the argument is somewhat separable and appeals to people across the political spectrum, including some libertarians and small-government conservatives.

Enforcement requires surveillance. Roughly 10–20% of recognized pregnancies end in miscarriage, and miscarriage and induced abortion are often clinically indistinguishable. Any enforcement regime therefore requires distinguishing them — which means investigating pregnancy loss. This has produced prosecutions of women for stillbirths and miscarriages (cases in Oklahoma, El Salvador, and elsewhere), subpoenas of medical records, data requests to period-tracking apps, and license-plate reader tracking of interstate travel. The argument is that the surveillance apparatus is not an unfortunate side effect but a structural necessity.

Precedent creep. Once the state has an interest in fetal welfare that overrides maternal consent, that interest doesn't logically confine itself to abortion. Proponents point to court-ordered cesareans, civil commitment of pregnant women with substance use disorders, and "fetal assault" statutes as evidence that the principle expands. National Advocates for Pregnant Women has documented well over a thousand such interventions.

Institutional distrust. The historical record of state control over reproduction includes compulsory sterilization upheld in Buck v. Bell, the Mississippi Appendectomy, and sterilization of Native American women through the Indian Health Service into the 1970s. The argument here is not that current legislators share those motives, but that the power — state authority over reproductive bodies — has a track record of being turned against the poor, disabled, and racial minorities regardless of the intentions with which it was created.

Epistemic humility. Legislatures are poorly equipped to adjudicate obstetric medicine. The decision involves the patient's health history, prognosis, values, religious convictions, family circumstances, and risk tolerance — information the state does not have and cannot obtain.

Claimed Benefits

  • Lower maternal mortality and morbidity, both from removing delays in emergency care and from the underlying fact that continued pregnancy is riskier than abortion.
  • Earlier care. Counterintuitively, proponents argue that removing gestational limits reduces later abortions, because restrictions, waiting periods, and provider scarcity are themselves a primary cause of delay.
  • No criminalization of pregnancy loss, and no chilling effect on patients seeking care after miscarriage.
  • Preserved clinical judgment. Physicians treat according to standard of care rather than legal risk calculus, and medical training in these procedures — needed for miscarriage management as well — is preserved.
  • Reduced inequality. Restrictions are least burdensome for those with money, flexibility, and mobility; a national floor of no restriction removes the geographic and class stratification of access.
  • Preservation of a general principle. The legal norm against compelled bodily use remains intact and unqualified, protecting everyone.
  • Non-imposition. Legal permission compels no one; those with moral objections remain free to decline, and to persuade rather than prohibit.

Internal Debates Within the Position

Even among adherents there are unresolved questions, which is worth noting for accuracy:

  • Whether the right is properly a right to end the pregnancy or a right to fetal demise. Thomson's argument, strictly applied, supports the former. If a fetus can be safely removed alive, some hold the autonomy claim is satisfied — others reject this as coercive and as ignoring the burdens of induction and the reality of genetic parenthood.
  • How to handle rare cases where a patient seeks abortion at, say, 38 weeks for non-medical reasons. Some bite the bullet on principle; others argue the case is so vanishingly rare and so likely to involve extremity that legislating for it is worse than the problem.
  • Whether "no restrictions" means no criminal restrictions specifically, versus no professional-standards regulation at all. Most proponents accept ordinary medical regulation (licensing, facility standards, informed consent) while rejecting abortion-specific criminal law.

What This Argument Doesn't Address

For completeness: critics contest the analogy between pregnancy and the violinist (voluntariness of most conception, the parent–child relationship, the difference between killing and letting die, the fact that gestation is what a body does rather than an extraordinary donation). They contest whether autonomy is genuinely lexically prior to another being's life. And they note that near-total permissiveness throughout gestation is well outside the global legal norm and outside majority public opinion in most countries, including the U.S., where support drops sharply by trimester. Those are real objections; the position above does not defeat them so much as decline to grant their premises.

The Only Body You Will Ever Own

Friends, neighbors, fellow citizens —

I want to begin with a question so simple that a child could answer it, and yet our laws still cannot: Who owns your body?

Not your body as a metaphor. Not your body as a symbol of the nation's virtue. Your actual body — the one you woke up in this morning, the one that carries you home tonight, the one that will one day fail you. Who owns it?

There is only one answer a free people can give. You do. You do, and no one else. Not your governor. Not your legislature. Not a judge who has never met you. Not a stranger with a sign outside a clinic door. Not a majority, however large, however sincere, however convinced of its own righteousness.

And if that is true — if it is truly, actually true — then we must stop pretending that it can be true most of the time, or up to a point, or until a committee says otherwise. Bodily autonomy is not a permission slip the state issues and revokes. It is either yours or it is not.

What Restriction Actually Means

We have grown so accustomed to the language of compromise that we've forgotten to look at what compromise costs, and who pays it.

A twenty-four-hour waiting period sounds reasonable in a legislative chamber. Now hear it from the other side: it means a woman who works two jobs and has no paid leave must find childcare twice, must find gas money twice, must find someone she trusts with her secret twice. It means the four-hour drive becomes an overnight stay she cannot afford. That is not reflection. That is a toll booth, and it is placed there precisely because someone hoped she would turn back.

A mandatory ultrasound and a scripted lecture sound like information. Hear it from the other side: it is the state seizing a doctor's mouth and using it to deliver a message the doctor knows to be manipulative. It is a woman strapped to a table and made to perform contrition for a decision she has already made with more seriousness than her legislators ever brought to anything.

A parental consent law sounds like family. Hear it from the other side: it is a frightened seventeen-year-old in a courtroom, before a judge, begging permission — because the reason she cannot tell her parents is the reason she needs help in the first place.

A gestational limit sounds like moderation. Hear it from the other side: it is a woman at twenty-two weeks learning that the pregnancy she wanted, the nursery she painted, the name she chose, will not survive — and being told that her state has decided her grief must also include a plane ticket.

Every restriction, without exception, falls hardest on the same people: the poor, the young, the rural, the abused, the undocumented, the ones with no savings and no flexibility and no lawyer. Wealth has always been able to buy its way past these laws. Restrictions do not end abortion. They ration it by class. They always have.

The Line We Cannot Draw

I know the objection. Surely somewhere there must be a limit. Surely we cannot mean no restrictions at all.

I mean exactly that — and here is why.

Every line we have ever drawn has been drawn by people who will never live on the wrong side of it. And every line, once drawn, becomes a weapon. Watch what happens the moment the law is permitted to sit in the exam room: doctors begin practicing medicine with one eye on the statute book. They wait. They hesitate. They ask a hospital lawyer whether a woman is dying enough yet. We have names now — real women, in real hospitals, in this century — who bled out in parking lots and waiting rooms while physicians consulted attorneys. That is not a hypothetical cost of "reasonable limits." That is the invoice, and it has been paid in blood.

There is no version of this where the state gets a little bit of jurisdiction over the pregnant body and uses it wisely. Give a legislature an inch of a woman's uterus and it will legislate the mile.

And so I say: leave the decision where it has always belonged — with the person whose body, whose life, whose future, whose health, whose family, whose faith, and whose conscience are actually at stake. She does not need a supervisor. She has been one all her life.

The Deeper Principle

Let me name the principle plainly, because I think we have been too shy about it.

We do not conscript bodies in this country. We do not harvest organs from the unwilling, even to save a life. We do not compel a father to donate bone marrow to his own dying child — and we are right not to, even as we grieve. Our law has understood, for a very long time, that no person may be commandeered as life support for another, no matter how sympathetic the need. The right to refuse the use of your body is not a loophole. It is bedrock.

Pregnancy is the one place we've made an exception. And the only thing that distinguishes it — the only thing — is who bears the burden.

That is not ethics. That is a double standard with a moral vocabulary borrowed for the occasion.

What Freedom Would Actually Look Like

So let us be ambitious, for once. Let us stop negotiating for a slightly less punitive cage.

Repeal the bans. All of them. Repeal the waiting periods, the forced scripts, the sham clinic regulations designed by people who could not name a single medical purpose they serve. Strike the criminal penalties that turn doctors into defendants and miscarriages into investigations. Take abortion out of the penal code entirely and put it where it belongs: in medicine, governed by the same standards of care, licensure, and consent that govern every other procedure a human being may choose.

And then — because a right you cannot reach is a right you do not have — fund it. Cover it. Train providers. Protect clinics. Make the freedom real in the places where it is currently a rumor.

The Ask

I am not asking you to feel a particular way about abortion. Feel what you feel. Believe what you believe. Teach it, preach it, live by it.

I am asking you for something narrower and much harder: to keep your hands off other people's bodies. To accept that a conviction sincerely held is still not a claim on someone else's flesh. To trust that the person facing the hardest decision of her life is more qualified to make it than you are — because she is.

Nine hundred years of law, a thousand years of scripture, and every legislature on earth have been arguing about the pregnant body. Almost none of them asked her.

Let us be the generation that finally does. Let us be the generation that says: your body, your life, your call — full stop, no exceptions, no permission required.

Not because it is easy. Because it is the only answer that treats her as a person.

Thank you.

The Unassailable Right: Why Absolute Bodily Autonomy Demands Unrestricted Abortion Access

The principle of bodily autonomy stands as one of the most fundamental pillars of human rights and liberal democratic society. It is the foundation upon which all other freedoms rest—the simple, powerful idea that individuals possess sovereign authority over their own bodies, and that no person or institution may compel the use of one's body against their will. This principle admits no exceptions, no compromises, and no government interference. If we are to take bodily autonomy seriously as a foundational right, we must logically extend it to its fullest expression: fully unrestricted abortion access at any stage of pregnancy, without exception.

The Indivisible Nature of Bodily Autonomy

Bodily autonomy is not a conditional right that applies only in convenient circumstances. We do not ask whether a person's reason for refusing organ donation is sufficiently compelling before we honor their refusal. We do not require a citizen to justify their decision to decline a blood transfusion, even if without it they will die. We understand that the right to control one's own body is absolute—it does not depend on the needs of others, the length of time a situation has persisted, or the moral judgments of third parties.

This absolute principle must apply equally to pregnancy. A pregnant person's body is their own, regardless of how many weeks have passed since conception. The duration of pregnancy cannot diminish the fundamental right to revoke consent to the use of one's bodily resources. To suggest that at some point in pregnancy this right evaporates is to assert that bodily autonomy is merely a privilege that the state may revoke at its discretion—a position that would undermine every other freedom we claim to hold dear.

The Problem of Forced Use of the Body

When the state prohibits abortion after a certain point in pregnancy, it is doing something extraordinary and deeply violent: it is compelling a person to continue providing their body as life support for another entity, against their explicit will. This is the only context in which Western law demands that one person sacrifice their bodily integrity for another. We do not force parents to donate kidneys to their dying children. We do not compel citizens to provide bone marrow to strangers. Yet in the case of pregnancy, the government claims the authority to force a person to undergo months of physical transformation, the risks of childbirth, and permanent bodily changes—all against their will.

This coercion is a profound violation of human dignity. The state is essentially saying to a pregnant person: "Your body no longer belongs entirely to you. We, the government, have determined that your bodily resources must be used to sustain another life, regardless of your wishes." This is the very definition of ownership—the state treating a person's body as a resource to be allocated according to its priorities.

Why Viability Is an Arbitrary and Irrelevant Distinction

Arguments for gestational limits often center on fetal "viability"—the point at which a fetus could potentially survive outside the womb with medical assistance. However, this distinction is morally irrelevant to the question of bodily autonomy. The ability of a fetus to survive with external support does not change the fundamental fact that the pregnant person is being forced to provide their body as the environment for that survival.

Consider this analogy: if a person is dying and requires the use of your kidneys to survive, their "viability" independent of you is irrelevant to your right to say no. Even if they could survive with someone else's kidneys, even if they are fully developed as a human being, you are not obligated to provide the use of your organs. The same logic applies in pregnancy. Whether or not a fetus could theoretically survive with neonatal intensive care does not alter the pregnant person's right to decline the continued use of their body.

Moreover, the viability threshold is technologically dependent and medically variable. It shifts with advances in medicine, differs between hospitals, and is subject to interpretation. A right that depends on the current state of medical technology is no right at all. True bodily autonomy must be absolute and non-contingent.

Addressing the "Life" Objection

The most common objection to unrestricted abortion access is the claim that a fetus is a human life deserving of protection. This objection fundamentally misunderstands the nature of rights. The right to life has never, in any other context, included the right to use another person's body against their will. Every person has a right to life, but no person has a right to someone else's organs, blood, or bodily resources—even if they will die without them.

The fetus' claim to life cannot override the pregnant person's claim to bodily autonomy, because bodily autonomy is the more fundamental right. It is the right upon which all other rights depend. To violate bodily autonomy to preserve life is to destroy the very foundation of rights in order to fulfill one specific right—a paradox that ultimately leaves no rights secure.

Furthermore, recognizing fetal personhood at any stage would have catastrophic implications for pregnant people, reducing them to mere vessels and establishing a legal precedent that some bodies are subject to state control. A society that can force pregnancy can force anything.

The Necessity of Absolute Protection

Partial restrictions—whether based on gestational age, fetal abnormalities, or any other criterion—inevitably create a system where some people's autonomy is protected while others' is denied. Such systems require the state to make moral judgments about which reasons for abortion are "valid" and which are not, a profoundly authoritarian approach to reproductive decision-making.

Only fully unrestricted access at any stage respects the principle that individuals, not governments, are the rightful authorities over their own bodies. Any compromise on this principle opens the door to further erosion of bodily autonomy. The history of reproductive rights demonstrates that restrictions never stop at "reasonable" boundaries—they create precedents that allow ever-greater encroachment.

Conclusion

Absolute bodily autonomy is not an extreme position; it is the only position that takes human rights seriously. The right to control one's own body is either absolute or it is nothing. If the government can force a person to remain pregnant against their will at any point, then bodily autonomy is merely a privilege that the state grants conditionally.

We must demand unrestricted abortion access at any stage of pregnancy, not because abortion is simple or morally uncomplicated, but because the alternative—government-mandated use of people's bodies—is slavery by another name. A just society does not legislate the use of unwilling bodies for any purpose, no matter how noble that purpose may seem. The body is the final frontier of human freedom, and it must remain inviolable.

Bodily Autonomy and the Unrestricted Right to Abortion

A Defense of Absolute Self-Sovereignty

The principle is deceptively simple, yet it sits at the foundation of what it means to be a free person: every human being has an inviolable right to determine what happens inside their own body. If this principle means anything, it means everything. If we accept it at all, we must accept it fully — without caveat, without graduated tiers of permission, and without government standing at a woman's bedroom door or operating table to veto her most intimate decisions.

This essay argues that abortion must be available without restriction at any stage of pregnancy, governed by nothing more than the pregnant person's own informed choice. The reasoning rests on three pillars: the absolute nature of bodily autonomy, the incoherence of drawing arbitrary gestational lines, and the destructive consequences of government interference in medical decisions.

I. The Body is the Last Dominion

Bodily autonomy is not a right that we hold provisionally. It is the right from which all other rights flow. Without sovereignty over your own flesh, your freedom of speech, your freedom of movement, and your freedom of conscience are merely permissions granted by the state — revocable the moment they become inconvenient.

If bodily autonomy is absolute, then no person can be compelled to use their body to sustain another — not even to save a life. The law does not force you to donate a kidney to a dying child, even though your child will certainly die without it. It does not compel you to surrender bone marrow, blood, or any organ, even when refusal means death for another consenting-dependent person. We recognize, rightly, that the right to refuse the use of one's body is so fundamental that it supersedes even the most compelling countervailing interest: human survival itself.

Pregnancy is an extraordinary biological undertaking. It transforms virtually every organ system. It carries risks of permanent injury, chronic illness, and death. To tell a woman that she must endure all of this — against her expressed will — because the state has decided her obligation outweighs her autonomy is not a nuanced policy position. It is conscription of the body. It is, in the most literal sense, forced servitude to another organism.

Those who argue that the pregnant person "assumed this responsibility" through voluntary sexual activity fundamentally misunderstand the nature of bodily rights. No voluntary act can morally or legally strip a person of their sovereignty over their own body. If it could, then we would be justified in forcing people to donate organs simply because they had ever met someone who needed one. Consent to sex — even fully informed, enthusiastic consent to unprotected sex — cannot constitute consent to pregnancy, any more than getting in a car constitutes consent to a collision. Bodies change course. Biology is not a contract.

II. The Incoherence of "Lines"

Opponents of unrestricted access invariably ask: But aren't there lines that must be drawn? They point to viability, to the third trimester, to fetal pain thresholds — searching for a philosophical event horizon at which the pregnant person's autonomy suddenly diminishes and the state's interest suddenly accelerates.

The problem is that every proposed line is arbitrary.

Viability is perhaps the most popular proposal, and the most philosophically bankrupt. Viability is not a fixed property of the fetus; it is a function of medical technology and geographic location. A fetus at 24 weeks may be "viable" in a major urban hospital with a Level IV NICU but will certainly die in a rural clinic without one. Should a woman's fundamental rights depend on her ZIP code? Should a neonatologist's capabilities override her autonomy? This is not a principle — it is an accident of engineering.

Birth is another commonly proposed line, but it solves nothing philosophically. At the moment of birth, the fetus becomes a person with full legal rights — but its dependence on a particular woman's body ceases. The woman can legally refuse to touch it, feed it, or shelter it. Once it is outside her body, the bodily autonomy question is resolved by sheer physics. Drawing the line at birth doesn't grant the fetal organism any different right before that moment; it merely ends the conflict of rights by removing the body from the equation. It tells us nothing about what happens when two entities must share one body.

Fetal pain, consciousness, and sentience are genuine scientific questions worth studying, but they cannot serve as principled lines, because they all involve degrees. Consciousness likely develops gradually. There is no toggle switch. And even if there were, it would only tell us something about the fetus's moral status — not about the pregnant person's obligation to gestate. We do not compel conscious, sentient, fully persons-alive in the world to donate sustainably compatible organs to each other. A higher capacity for suffering compels us to extend moral consideration — but it does not grant anyone the right to commandeer another person's body against their will.

Every line drawn between conception and birth is, at its foundation, an assertion that some point the state's interest in potential life overwhelms the actual, living, breathing person's interest in self-determination. But no coherent non-arbitrary argument exists for why this tipping point occurs at week 12 rather than week 8, at week 24 rather than week 30, or at any other moment. The line moves with technology, culture, and politics, which is exactly what should alarm anyone who thinks of rights as something more than legislative convenience.

The only non-arbitrary line is the only meaningful one: the body itself. Before that line, no one has a right to it. After that line, the conflict ends because the dependency ends.

III. The Destructiveness of Restriction

Even if one remains unpersuaded on pure principle, the practical consequences of restricting abortion provide their own devastating argument.

Restrictions do not end abortion — they end safe abortion. The data is unambiguous and globally consistent. Before Roe v. Wade, an estimated 200,000 to 1.2 million illegal abortions occurred annually in the United States. Women died of sepsis, hemorrhage, and perforation. They died because they had no legal option, because the state decided it knew better than they did what should happen inside their bodies. The Guttmacher Institute, the World Health Organization, and decades of public health research confirm what should be obvious: making abortion illegal regulates its safety, never its incidence.

Restrictions create a two-tiered system of justice. Wealthy women will always find a way. They will travel, they will have connections, they will access private physicians. Abortion bans fall with crushing, disproportionate force on the poor, on rural populations, on teenagers, on victims of rape and incest, on women whose pregnancies threaten their health in ways that don't meet the narrow exceptions legislatures grudgingly carve out. Abortion restrictions are, in practice, class warfare fought on women's bodies.

Restrictions corrupt the doctor-patient relationship. When physicians must consult attorneys before providing care, when pharmacists must verify legal permissibility before dispensing medication, when hospital review boards second-guess medical judgment — the result is not "protective medicine." It is bureaucratic terror. Doctors stop providing perfectly legal care out of fear. Women in emergency situations — ectopic pregnancies, incomplete miscarriages, sepsis — suffer and die while administrators determine whether their treatment fits within the allowed exceptions. The Dobbs era has already produced documented cases of women being denied standard-of-care miscarriage management because the treatment (a D&C or medication identical to abortion care) exists in a legal gray zone. This is not the byproduct of well-meaning regulation. This is the predictable consequence of legislating medicine.

IV. Addressing the Objections

"But what about the fetus?"

This is the most serious objection, and it deserves a serious answer. The question of the fetus's moral status is genuinely complex, and people of good faith disagree. But the resolution of that debate cannot be that the pregnant person loses her bodily autonomy. If the fetus is a full person with full rights, we have a rights conflict — just as we would if two adults were surgically joined and one needed the other's body to survive. And just as in that hypothetical case, the law has never compelled one person to sustain another against their will.

One's view of the fetus's moral status may deepen the emotional weight of the decision. It does not change the ethical framework. People make agonizing decisions about their bodies every day in contexts large and small. We do not therefore grant the state authority to make those decisions for them.

"Isn't there a societal interest in protecting potential life?"

Societies have many interests, but no interest is powerful enough to override fundamental constitutional and human rights. The state has an interest in the health of its citizens too — yet it cannot force you to eat a healthy diet, exercise, or quit smoking. It has an interest in the lives of organ failure patients — yet it cannot open your body without consent. Potential future citizens, however valued, cannot claim rights that actual living citizens do not possess.

"What about late-term abortion? Isn't that extreme?"

Late-term abortions are extraordinarily rare — roughly 1% of all abortions in the United States, according to the CDC. They are almost always performed in the context of devastating circumstances: severe fetal anomalies incompatible with life, grave threats to the pregnant person's health, or catastrophic changes in circumstance that prevented earlier access. The women and families involved are enduring some of the worst experiences a human being can face. They do not need the additional torment of a politician who has never met them declaring that they should have been faster, smarter, or more deserving.

The principle that a woman can make this decision with her doctor, based on the facts of her own life and body, without a committee of legislators second-guessing her tragedy — this is not extremism. This is basic human decency.

V. What Absolute Autonomy Requires

Accepting absolute bodily autonomy as the governing principle demands that we accept several uncomfortable conclusions:

  1. No government — federal, state, or local — should have the authority to restrict, regulate, delay, or condition abortion access at any gestational stage.

  2. No waiting periods, no mandatory counseling, no ultrasound-viewing requirements. These are not neutral medical practices. They are state-engineered psychological obstacles designed to plant seeds of doubt and guilt. They communicate, from the government to the patient: We don't think you mean what you're saying. We think we can change your mind. This is coercion dressed in clinical language.

  3. No gestational limits that functionally deny access. Restrictions on "late-term" abortions that are written with narrow or no exceptions effectively ban the care that the most vulnerable patients need most. If you truly respect autonomy, you cannot build an exception system so narrow that it fails the people who need it most.

  4. No parental consent or notification requirements for minors. These do not protect young people. They delay care, push minors toward later-stage procedures, and in abusive households, they place children in danger. The teenager carrying an unwanted pregnancy already faces enormous obstacles. Adding a requirement that they disclose to their parent or obtain a judicial waiver — often in a town where the court clerk goes to their church — is not protection. It is punishment.

  5. No restrictions on medication abortion. Medication abortion accounts for the majority of abortions in the United States and is safer than common drugs like Viagra and Tylenol. Efforts to restrict access to mifepristone and misoprostol are not rooted in legitimate safety concerns. They are political attacks on the single most accessible form of reproductive care, aimed primarily at women in rural and underserved areas.

VI. The Deeper Principle

Beneath this policy debate lies a question that is almost religious in its weight: Who owns your body?

If the answer is you, then the conclusion is inescapable. You may choose to continue a pregnancy out of love, faith, or personal commitment. You may choose to end one out of love for the children you already have, compassion for a wanted but fatally anomalous fetus, pragmatic recognition that you cannot support a child, or simply the unshakeable knowledge that you do not want to be pregnant. These are all acts of moral agency — different, complex, sometimes painful — and they are all yours.

If the answer is someone else — the state, the church, the fetus, the biological father, society at large — then the principle of bodily autonomy is a lie we tell ourselves, and women are not fully free people. They are vessels with conditional rights, granted access to self-determination only when aligned with someone else's priorities.

The only honest position is the first one. And once you accept it, you must follow it to its end.

Conclusion

Unrestricted abortion access is not a radical fringe position. It is the logical, consistent, and morally necessary conclusion of the most basic liberal democratic principle: that the individual is sovereign over their own body, and that government power must have clear limits when it seeks to invade the most personal and intimate domain of human experience.

Drawing lines, building exceptions, and creating tiers of restricted access are not compromises. They are the architecture of subjugation, constructed by politicians who will never face the consequences of the laws they write. Every hour of delay, every bureaucratic barrier forced between a woman and her doctor, every judicial proceeding that substitutes a judge's judgment for her own — these are violations of a fundamental human right.

The body is the last, most essential territory of the self. No government has a right to occupy it. No legislator has a right to command it. No fetus, however potential its life, has a right to sustain itself within it against the will of the person whose blood, whose organs, whose life are carrying it forward.

Bodily autonomy is not a spectrum. It is a wall. And on the other side of that wall, the state must stop.
